{{Short description|Concept in quadratic forms}}
{{distinguish|Hermite normal form}}
In the theory of [[quadratic form]]s, a '''Hermite reduction''' of a real [[positive definite form]] is another real positive definite form integrally equivalent to it whose coefficients are reasonably small in the sense defined below.

== Definition ==
A [[positive definite form]]
:<math>Q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nQ_{ij}x_ix_j</math>
on <math>\mathbb R^n</math> is '''Hermite reduced''' if the following recursively defined condition is satisfied.
* <math>0<|Q_{11}|\le(4/3)^{(n-1)/2}\sqrt[n]{\det Q}</math>
* <math>2|Q_{1i}|\le|Q_{11}|\qquad(i=2,\dots,n)</math>
* The form <math>Q'(x_2,\dots,x_n)=Q_{11}Q(x)-(Q_{11}x_1+\cdots+Q_{1n}x_n)^2</math> is a Hermite reduced form on <math>\mathbb R^{n-1}</math>

For every [[positive definite form]] <math>Q</math> on <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, there exists a <math>\mathbb Z</math>-module isomorphism <math>U\colon\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z^n</math> and a Hermite reduced form <math>\tilde Q</math> on <math>\mathbb R^n</math> such that<ref name="Cassels">{{cite book |last=Cassels |first=J. W. S. |author-link=J. W. S. Cassels |title=Rational quadratic forms |language=en |series=London Mathematical Society Monographs |volume=13 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London–New York |date=1978 |mr=0522835 |zbl=0395.10029}}</ref>{{rp|259}}<ref name="Grosswald">{{cite book |last=Grosswald |first=Emil |title=Representations of integers as sums of squares |language=en |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |date=1985 |isbn=978-1-4613-8568-4 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8566-0 |mr=0803155 |zbl=0574.10045}}</ref>{{rp|210}}<ref name="CIM">{{cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Wai Kiu |last2=Icaza |first2=María Inés |title=Hermite reduction and a Waring’s problem for integral quadratic forms over number fields |language=en |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=374 |issue=4 |pages=2967–2985 |date=2021 |issn=0002-9947 |doi=10.1090/tran/8298 |mr=4223039 |zbl=1465.11091 |arxiv=2007.06454}}</ref>
:<math>Q\circ(U\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R)=\tilde Q.</math>
In matrix notation, for every real <math>n\times n</math> [[positive definite matrix]] <math>Q</math>, there exists an integer <math>n\times n</math> [[invertible matrix]] <math>U</math> (so-called [[unimodular matrix]]) and an <math>n\times n</math> Hermite reduced matrix <math>\tilde Q</math> such that
:<math>U^TQU=\tilde Q.</math>
Then <math>\tilde Q</math> is called a '''Hermite reduction''' of <math>Q</math>.

Each real positive definite form has only a finite number of Hermite reductions; they are not unique in general.

== Application ==
The Hermite reduction of a binary or ternary positive definite form with integer coefficients with determinant 1 is simply the sum of squares. This is used in a proof of [[Legendre's three-square theorem]]: to show that an integer is a sum of squares of three integers it is sufficient to show that it can be represented by a ternary positive definite form with determinant 1.

== Historical note ==
The Hermite reduction is named after [[Charles Hermite]].
